question: Consider the matrices $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$, $B=[5]$ and $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2\\3&1&4\end{bmatrix}$. Identify the matrices for which determinants exist and evaluate those determinants. Justify why the remaining determinant is not defined.
explanation:
Condition for the existence of a determinant
A determinant is defined only for a square matrix, in which the number of rows equals the number of columns.
Determinant of $A$
The matrix $A$ is square and has order $2$. Therefore, $$|A|=(1)(4)-(2)(3)=4-6=-2$$
Determinant of $B$
The matrix $B$ has order $1$. Hence, its determinant equals its only element: $$|B|=5$$
Examination of $C$
The matrix $C$ has order $2\times3$. Since it is not square, $|C|$ is not defined.
Thus, the determinants of $A$ and $B$ are $-2$ and $5$, respectively, while the determinant of $C$ does not exist.

options.A: Determinants exist for $A$ and $B$: $|A|=-2$, $|B|=5$; $|C|$ is not defined because $C$ is non-square.
options.B: Determinants exist for $A$ and $C$: $|A|=-2$, $|C|=4$; $|B|$ is not defined because $B$ has order $1$.
options.C: Determinants exist only for $A$: $|A|=2$; $|B|$ and $|C|$ are not defined.
options.D: Determinants exist for all three matrices: $|A|=-2$, $|B|=5$, $|C|=0$.
